name: Nyulnyul
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

catalog_quote: As in most Australian languages, stress is not phonemic in Nyulnyul: it does not serve a contrastive function, and no words are distinguished by different loci of stress. Rather, the function of stress is primarily delimitative, that is, it marks the location of word boundaries (Trubetzkoy 1969:27). However, it does not seem to achieve this function completely consistently either, as stress does not appear to be completely predictable, and, as in many other Nyulnyulan languages, there are words that are not stressed according to the regular pattern. ... a phonological word is a single unit in regard to stress placement; it is a phonological unit over which stress is assigned regularly. The first syllable of a phonological word is accorded stress. One or more subsequent syllables may be stressed also; this must be an odd numbered syllable, provided that its vowel is not at the right edge of the word. In other words, an odd numbered syllable is stressed only if it is strong, or it is followed by at least one more syllable. ... As in the majority of Australian languages the first syllable of a free root is normally assigned stress. ... Bisyllabic simple roots ... have just a single stressed syllable, the initial syllable, as in 'ba.barl ‘brother’ ... Trisyllabic roots also have stress on their initial syllable ... If a trisyllabic word ends in a consonant or consonant cluster, the final syllable also takes stress: 'ka.rriny.'kam ‚root vegetable type‛, 'wam.ba.'rrird ‘yam’

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (966 PDF pages, text present; extracted text). p. 132 carries the running header "100 Chapter 3", so the locator (printed p. 100 = p. 132) is exact; §3.4 Stress runs printed pp. 98-107 = pp. 130-139 as stated. The quoted passage is on p. 100 verbatim: "As in most Australian languages, stress is not phonemic in Nyulnyul: it does not serve a contrastive function, and no words are distinguished by different loci of stress. Rather, the function of stress is primarily delimitative, that is, it marks the location of word boundaries (Trubetzkoy 1969:27). However, it does not seem to achieve this function completely consistently either, as stress does not appear to be completely predictable.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and marks word edges. The first syllable of every phonological word (free root, each reduplicant, each compound member, each non-coherent suffix/clitic, and each of the two p-words of an inflecting verb: prefix complex vs root+suffixes) is stressed; further stresses go on odd-numbered syllables (3rd, 5th) if they are 'strong' (>2 morae or word-initial) or are followed by another syllable, so a trisyllabic consonant-final root is stressed 1st+3rd ('ka.rriny.'kam) while a vowel-final one is stressed only initially ('ba.ba.rli). The author stresses that the pattern is not fully predictable and rests on one deaf speaker.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Degrees of stress could not be distinguished in the data; all stressed syllables are marked alike with the primary-stress symbol. Additional (non-initial) stresses fall on the 3rd and 5th syllables in 4-6 syllable roots when strong or non-final ('ku.rru.'lu.kun, 'wi.da.'ma.nga.'ran); in prefixed nouns the third syllable ('nga.la.'bab). In inflected verbs stress may shift from the 1st to the 2nd syllable of the prefix complex to yield an alternating rhythm ('i.ngi.rra.'man ~ i.'ngi.rra.'man). Nekes & Worms (2006:67, as reported by McGregor) said secondary accent sometimes on the fourth syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Some words are consistently non-initially stressed: kudaarrawany 'brolga' ku.'daa.rra.'wany (2nd+4th, heavy 2nd syllable); bisyllables with a heavier second syllable ka.'rdimb, ka.'lamb, ku.'narr; prefixed nouns ni.'mirl, ni.'many, ni.'ma.rraj; verb -BAKAND 'have' always on its 2nd syllable; roots di.'wirl.'wirl, ji.'bily.'bily where a sub-bimoraic element outside a reduplication is unstressed; a strong final syllable may take the second stress instead of a weak third ('ka.ja.na.'ngurr); compound wamb-uriny stressed as one root 'wam.bu.'riny; free alternation of 1st/2nd-syllable stress in monosyllabic-root verb forms (i.'li-j, wa.'na-w). Author: 'stress does not appear to be completely predictable'.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word, defined by stress assignment (§2.4, §3.4); d-words normally = p-words. Isolated-word stress does not always match sentential stress; a certain amount of shifting occurs, attributed to discourse rhythm. Analysis based exclusively on the deaf speaker's recordings (isolated words and texts); pitch and length are independent of stress; strength (mora count) interferes with stress perception.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Nyulnyul proper (Beagle Bay / Dampier Land), the language-level languoid nyul1247; no dialect split. The stress analysis rests exclusively on recordings of one late speaker (Mary Carmel Charles, deaf), so the author flags it as incomplete. The only earlier statement (Nekes & Worms [1953] 2006:67, reported second-hand in McGregor 2011:98 fn. 18) gives first-syllable accent with occasional secondary accent on the fourth syllable.

sources.note: §3.4 Stress (pp. 98-107, pp. 130-139): stress non-phonemic and delimitative; the first syllable of a phonological word is stressed, further stresses on odd-numbered syllables that are strong or non-final; irregular words (kudaarrawany 2nd+4th; ka.'rdimb, ka.'lamb, ku.'narr second-syllable when heavier); reduplicants, compounds, non-coherent suffixes/clitics stressed as separate p-words; inflected verbs split into two p-words with optional rhythmic stress shift; -BAKAND 'have' always stressed on 2nd syllable; degrees of stress not distinguishable in the data.
